newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protests continue despite election decision.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protests continue despite election decision.

text.p: Thousands of students marched in Belgrade on Wednesday as demonstrations continued in Serbia despite the passage of a law reversing an election fraud that had sparked months of protests.

The students and opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, in the face of concern that continuing protests could raise tensions, said they would keep up the pressure on autocratic Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic to meet other demands.
"We shall not leave the protests until all demands are met," said Miodrag Gavrilovic, one of the leaders of 15,000 students who marched unhindered by police through the streets of the capital.
The students, among their demands, want the Belgrade University rector and a student co-rector sacked while one of Zajedno's demands is for greater access to strictly-controlled state media.
"I expect protests to continue in all of Serbia until larger changes than the return of stolen votes happen," said Zoran Djindjic, one of the three Zajedno leaders.

Zajedno planned to try to keep up enthusiasm for its daily protest rallies, now in their 12th week, by launching a red boat in the Danube River on Wednesday evening, to symbolically say farewell to ruling Socialists "who are leaving Belgrade".

The protests continued despite the passing on Tuesday of a special law by the Socialist-dominated parliament at the behest of Milosevic reinstating Zajedno's annulled victories in 14 cities in November elections.
The parliament's action, after three months of daily protests and widespread international condemnation of the Serbian government, was welcomed with caution by Britain, France and Germany.
"This is an important step in the right direction. The law has been voted, now it must be applied," French foreign ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters in Paris.

Zajedno, wrong-footed on numerous occasions by the government in legal ploys over the November elections, was cautious about declaring the electoral battle over until Zajedno councillors are installed, which could take from three to 10 days.
Meanwhile the neo-communist Yugoslav United Left (JUL) party, a hardline ruling coalition partner, warned against moves to topple the government by the street protests.

"I don't understand, do they (opposition) expect the police and the state to do nothing in their defence?" Belgrade VIP newsletter quoted JUL spokesman Aleksandar Vulin as saying in an interview with Belgrade's Nedeljni Telegraf.
The West has cautioned Milosevic against using force against peaceful demonstrators and to open dialogue with his rivals, notably on the issues of access to the media.
In return Zajedno leaders have reportedly promised to the West they would cease testing Milosevic's patience on the streets once their victories were reinstated.

The United States has retained a crippling outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade, barring access to desperately needed foreign capital until it improves its human rights record and shows genuine commitment to democracy.
Starved for fresh cash, with wages and pensions running late in an election year, Milosevic has repeatedly promised reforms but few among the opposition believe they will happen.
Against such a backdrop, Djindjic warned popular discontent might assume a life of its own beyond Zajedno control.
"The mood is extremely tense, people are not satisifed with crumbs. On the contrary, they are prepared regardless of the parliament decision to continue protesting.
"I think that we will enter a new stage which will be dictated by the people and not parties. It will be a stage of tough fighting for reforms and changes," he said.
